recognized_text: Sir, a new field file from planet earth, the network file. Report one, the mobile phone. The thing in every human pocket. Just over 8 billion humans and almost 9 billion phone lines, more lines than humans. The owners? Only about 6 billion. So many carry two or three lines and answer one. Today, how a voice gets from pocket to pocket, why it's called cellular and why it dies in elevators. Strangest part? Almost none of them know where their voice goes every day. Never wondered. A human talks, the air shakes, the microphone turns the shaking into an electric wave. The phone measures that wave thousands of times a second. On a normal call, 8,000. Why 8,000? Human speech doesn't need more. Music needs a lot more. which is why hold music sounds that terrible. Each measurement becomes a number. The wave is done. Only the numbers travel. Then it squeezes them, dropping what human ears won't miss. So, what arrives isn't your voice, sir. It's a summary. Then out they go, into the air. Into the air how? First surprise, a mobile isn't a phone. A mobile is a radio. Humans can see light. Radio is the same kind of wave, same speed. Just longer and invisible to them. So, each one carries a tiny radio station, sending and receiving at the same time. Not just one. Station one, the tower. Wi-Fi radio two, the earbuds radio three. Location listens to satellites, that's four. Airplane mode does exactly one thing. It silences them all. One human waiting for a bus beams four signals. The planet is drowning in waves they can't see. I can, sir. It's a mess. Second surprise, that wave doesn't go far, just to the nearest tower, a few hundred meters. From the tower, it drops into an underground cable to the core, a building full of computers. The core finds the other phone and cables it to her nearest tower. The cord does three things. Knows who you are, knows where the other one is, and bills you. Only the third never goes down. In the last few hundred meters, radio again. So wireless is wireless only at both ends, sir. The middle is all wires. The most wired thing on the planet and they call it wireless. All in under a quarter second. She hears him before he finishes the sentence. So why cellular? Because their land is cut into cells. Each cell has a tower. The trick? Channels in the air are limited. Each cell gets a set and cells that don't touch reuse it. The same air sold a thousand times. City cells are tiny, a tower every few streets. Desert cells can span tens of kilometers. Each tower has antennas facing every way. A phone signal is weaker than a tiny bulb. The tower has big ears. Weak signal? The phone shouts to be heard. That's why batteries die fast where coverage is bad. Cities hate how towers look, so they disguise them as palms. A poor disguise, sir. Honestly, better than mine. The key fact for any spy, a silent phone keeps whispering to the nearest tower, "I'm here." It has to. How else would a call find it? From the signal at nearby towers, the network works out roughly where it is. No satellites needed. So the network always knows where they are. They pay monthly for a tracking device and complain when the data runs out. In a moving car, the call is handed from tower to tower in a split second. He never notices. And when the handover fails, "Hello?" Hello, can you hear me? The most spoken sentence in this planet's history. How does it know who you are? The SIM, plastic the size of a fingernail. The SIM is you, not the phone. Move it and your number moves too. It holds a secret key the network use of to check it's not a copy. The newest ones aren't plastic at all. They're built into the phone. The phone has its own serial number, so a stolen one can be locked. The phone number is an address. First digits the country, next the company. The rest you. The network reads it like a mail carrier reads an envelope. Travel abroad and your phone finds a foreign network and introduces itself. The foreign network asks home, "One of yours?" Yours says, "Yes, and he'll pay." He'll pay a lot. All their networks talk and bill each other. Some countries won't speak at all, yet their networks get along. Money unites sir. Why do calls drop? Reason one, distance. The farther from the tower, the weaker the wave. Reason two, walls. Concrete and steel swallow the wave. Three, the elevator. A sealed metal box, the best radio shield they ever built. And they ride it mid-call. Four, crowds. A tower serves only so many. At a match, everyone's on their phone and the tower says, "Enough." Those bars on the screen measure signal, not how busy the tower is. Five bars, nothing loads? The bars are just to calm them. To be fair, in many countries the emergency number works without a SIM on any network. First time I've seen them agree on something useful. Before cells, there were car phones. One tall tower for the whole city with a few channels. A few calls at once for an entire city. Everyone else waited their turn. So the idea of cells made the mobile, not the device. It began on April 3rd, 1973. An engineer named Martin Cooper stood on a New York sidewalk and made the first call from a handheld phone. Who did he call? His rival, a guy at company racing him, to say, "I'm calling from the street." The planet's first mobile call was a taunt. I respect this being. It weighed over a kilo. 10 hours to charge for half an hour of talk. Sold 10 years later, it cost about $4,000. The first commercial network opened in Tokyo in 79. First generation, voice only. Anyone with a radio could listen in. Second generation, 91, the voice became numbers and texting came along. The first text was sent in December 92. It said, "Merry Christmas." Texts had 160 characters squeezed into a spare gap in the network signals. Humans invented a whole slang for a spare slot. Three put the internet in the phone. Four made everything internet. Even the voice. In 5 from 2019, much faster. And not just for humans, for machines talking to machines. Each generation humans say, "This will change our lives." What actually changes, they watch the same videos in higher quality. Today, 5G covers more than half the planet's people, but not fairly. Rich countries, 84%; poor countries, 4. Latest development, the towers will went to space. Since 2025, an ordinary phone can text a satellite directly. No dish, no special gear. Desert, sea, anywhere that can see the sky. It flies hundreds of kilometers up at 27,000 km/h, and a pocket phone talks to it. My ship can't do that, sir. Calls are still being tested, but soon nowhere on this planet will be out of range. Bad news for us, sir. I used to hide there. Two words from the human dictionary. Cell, the area one tower covers. That's where cell phone comes from. And SIM, the card that holds your identity. They lose it more often than their house keys. Summary, sir. One, the mobile is a radio that reaches only the nearest tower. Two, everything else is cables. Three, the network must know where you are to reach you. One question remains. Where do those cables go? And where does this internet actually live? Next report, the internet. The answer, sir, is on the seabed. This has been Earth Report, Agent Peak. End of transmission.
